label: Hidden Variables and EM
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 179 through 189 and treats observed data as a shadow of richer complete data. The EM algorithm fills in a compatible hidden-variable distribution, then refits the visible model. We will read both steps as alternating geometric projections between two manifolds.

label: Complete Data and Its Shadow
notes: A hidden-variable model carries complete data x and z, but observation exposes only x. The missing label z enlarges the complete-data space, and the observed law is a marginal. Inference must recover model parameters while the latent coordinate remains unseen, which is exactly what makes the likelihood awkward.

label: EM as Alternating Projection
notes: Place complete-data distributions in a large ambient simplex. The data manifold collects every completion that marginalizes to what we saw; the model manifold is the parametric family lifted to complete data. EM alternates projections between these two sets, zig-zagging toward their meeting point rather than following a straight path.

label: The E-Step: m-Projection
notes: The E-step holds the current parameter fixed and chooses hidden conditionals from the model, completing the empirical distribution. Geometrically this is an m-projection that lands on the data manifold. In a Gaussian mixture it produces responsibilities: the conditional probability that each observed point came from each component.

label: The M-Step: e-Projection
notes: The M-step holds the completed empirical distribution fixed and finds the model point closest to it, maximizing the expected complete-data log likelihood. Geometrically this is an e-projection back onto the model manifold. For a mixture it reduces to responsibility-weighted means and variances, the same updates a known label would give.

label: Free Energy and KL Decomposition
notes: Introduce a variational distribution q over hidden variables. The observed log likelihood splits into a free-energy bound plus a non-negative KL gap between q and the true posterior. The E-step zeroes that gap; the M-step raises the bound. This decomposition is the engine behind every monotonicity claim.

label: Monotone Likelihood Ascent
notes: Because each step solves a local projection that never decreases the bound, the observed log likelihood rises until improvement becomes negligible. The notebook trace climbs from roughly minus six hundred and saturates. EM is a local method: each step is principled, but multimodality and label switching mean the starting point still matters.

label: Responsibilities and Missing Information
notes: On the mixture boundary responsibilities are nearly zero or one, so labels are almost known. In the overlap band the same point fits both components, and that fuzziness is missing information made visible. Observed information is smaller than complete information because curvature is spent explaining label uncertainty.

label: Data Processing and KL Contraction
notes: Hidden variables are a non-invertible observation map; coarse-graining that merges states is another. KL divergence cannot increase under such many-to-one maps. The notebook collapses six states into three bins and watches the divergence shrink. A statistic is sufficient exactly when this loss vanishes for the family in question.

label: Misspecification as KL Projection
notes: A hidden-variable model can still be wrong. Fit one fixed-variance Gaussian to two-component mixture data and the best mean is not a component mean; it is the KL projection of the truth onto the restricted family, namely the mixture average. Misspecification redefines the estimation target as the closest available model point.

label: Recap and Sanity Checks
notes: EM lifts the problem to complete data, then alternates an m-projection E-step and an e-projection M-step, ascending the observed likelihood via the free-energy and KL decomposition. The notebook verifies normalized responsibilities, a monotone trace, KL contraction, and a misspecified projection landing near the mixture mean.
